summary: Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) are the rules that decide which identifier labels are valid and which alternative forms, called variants, are related, as in Internationalized Domain Names. This document gives guidance on how to design LGRs that handle variant labels sensibly.

eli5.summary: Some words can be written in more than one way that look or mean the same. This gives rule-makers advice on how to treat those look-alike spellings fairly.

subtitle: Designing rules for variant labels in internationalized domain names.

tldr.problem: Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) define which identifier labels are valid in systems like Internationalized Domain Names. Many labels have variant forms that look or mean the same (like 'rn' and 'm' in some fonts, or accented and unaccented versions of letters). Deciding when variants should be allocatable, blocked, or reserved is complex and error-prone without clear design principles.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides a framework for designing LGRs with well-behaved variant specifications. It introduces concepts like variant type sets, allocatable and blocked dispositions, conditional variants (which apply only in certain positions), and subtypes to limit the combinatorial explosion of variant labels. It shows how to ensure variant rules are symmetric and transitive, which keeps implementations simple.
tldr.outcome: LGR designers can create specifications that are predictable, reliable, and easier to implement and verify. The techniques balance the security goal of protecting registrants from confusable variants with the practical need to keep the number of allocatable variants manageable.

facts.label: Variant unit
facts.value: Code points or code point sequences

today: RFC 8228 is Informational and provides best-practice guidance for designing LGRs. It remains current as a reference for implementers of Internationalized Domain Name systems and other identifier registries that must manage variant labels.

sections.title: The Variant Problem
sections.content:
Label Generation Rulesets (LGRs) are the rules that decide which identifier labels are valid. They are used in systems like Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), where labels can contain characters from many scripts and languages. Beyond simply validating labels, LGRs can identify variant labels: alternate forms that are visually or semantically indistinguishable in a given script.

A variant label is neither merely similar nor just a typo. It represents a form of equivalence. For example, in some scripts, the letter 'rn' (r followed by n) looks identical to the letter 'm' at small screen sizes. In others, accented and unaccented versions of a letter are visually interchangeable in casual reading. The challenge is deciding the disposition of each variant: should it be allocatable (available to the same registrant as the original), blocked (reserved and unavailable to anyone else), or something else?

Correctly defining variants improves security by protecting registrants from confusable alternatives being registered by others, but poorly designed variants can create ambiguities, unintended allocations, and complicated implementation logic.
sections.eli5: Different ways to write the same letter (like with or without an accent mark) can look the same. The rules need to decide fairly which versions a single person can register together and which versions stay separate.

sections.title: Variants as Equivalence Relations
sections.content:
At its core, a variant relation is a 'same as' relation. If A is the same as B, then B is the same as A (symmetry), and if B is also the same as C, then A is the same as C (transitivity). This is called an equivalence relation, and it has powerful implications for implementation.

For example, if the character A is a variant of B, and B is a variant of C, then A and C must also be variants. When rules satisfy both symmetry and transitivity, variant labels that are mutual variants form disjoint sets: no label in one set is a variant of any label in another. This property makes it very fast for registries to check whether a new application conflicts with already-registered variants.

Not all relations are transitive. For instance, visual confusability is not: two labels can each look confusingly similar to a third without looking similar to each other (imagine a shape that is 'between' two other shapes). The RFC explicitly limits discussion to symmetric and transitive relations because of their implementation benefits, though it notes that mechanically verifying symmetry and transitivity is straightforward.
sections.eli5: If X and Y are the same, and Y and Z are the same, then X and Z have to be the same too. This rule makes everything simpler and faster for the system.

sections.title: Variant Mappings and Dispositions
sections.content:
An LGR is not defined in terms of labels but in terms of code points (the numeric values for characters). The LGR specifies which code points (or sequences of code points) can map to which others. When you generate all possible variant labels from an original, you are essentially replacing each code point according to these mappings.

Each mapping is labeled with a type: 'allocatable' or 'blocked' are the two main types, though custom subtypes can be defined. When an applicant applies for a label like 'AAA' (three A's), the system generates all permutations using variant mappings and determines the disposition of each permutation. If A maps to O with type 'allocatable', then both 'AAA' and 'OOO' can be allocated to the same registrant. If A maps to B with type 'blocked', then 'BBB' is reserved and not available to anyone.

The disposition of a variant label is determined by looking at the variant types used to create it. A label created only using 'allocatable' mappings is allocatable. A label that uses any 'blocked' mapping is blocked. This decision logic is flexible and can be customized using derivation conditions expressed as rules in XML.
sections.eli5: You define which characters can be swapped for each other, and mark each swap as either 'available to register together' or 'locked away from everyone else'. When you generate all possible spellings, the marking determines what happens to each one.

sections.title: Managing Complexity: Pure Variants and Subtypes
sections.content:
Without constraints, the number of variant labels explodes combinatorially. A label with three code points, each having two allocatable variants, generates 2^3 = 8 variant labels. For longer labels or more variants per code point, the count becomes unmanageable. The RFC introduces techniques to control this explosion.

The 'only-variants' qualifier requires that a variant label use only variant mappings (no original code points), which eliminates mixed forms like 'AOA' when starting from 'AAA'. Reflexive variants (a code point mapping to itself) can be assigned a type, ensuring that the disposition logic applies consistently even when a code point is unchanged. This matters when using the 'only-variants' condition: without reflexive variants, a mixed form would incorrectly appear to have the same disposition as a pure variant.

For more control, variant mappings can be grouped into subtypes (like 'simplified' and 'traditional' in Chinese). Derivation rules can then enforce that labels only mix certain subtypes, preventing incompatible variants from being allocated together while keeping others allocatable as long as they respect subtype boundaries.
sections.eli5: Instead of allowing every possible mix of swaps, you can say 'this group of swaps can go together, but that group cannot'. This keeps the number of registerable variations reasonable.

sections.title: Conditional and Out-of-Repertoire Variants
sections.content:
Some scripts have letters that change shape depending on their position in a word. In cursive scripts like Arabic, a letter looks different at the start, middle, and end of a word. A variant mapping may apply only in certain positions; for example, two code points might have the same final form but different initial forms. The RFC calls these conditional variants and shows how to express them with context conditions like 'final' or '!final'.

Conditional variants add complexity and require careful design to remain well-behaved. The context must be stable: if two code points are variants only in final position, that relationship must be true in both the original label and in any variant label. The RFC advises that conditional contexts be used sparingly and only when unconditional rules cannot achieve the design goal.

Another edge case is out-of-repertoire variants: defining variant mappings to code points that are not part of the LGR's repertoire. This is useful when multiple LGRs interact and a label valid in one should be blocked in another. Such mappings require special handling via a reflexive 'out-of-repertoire-var' type to ensure they are marked invalid when encountered.
sections.eli5: Some letters look the same only at the end of a word, not at the beginning. Or you might want to block a variant that comes from a different script's rules. Both cases need special care.

sections.title: Well-Behaved LGRs and XML Representation
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that a 'well-behaved' LGR is one that is predictable to its author and reviewer and reliable in its implementation. Beyond what the schema formally requires, a well-behaved LGR actively avoids ambiguities: situations where the intended disposition of a variant is unclear or where different implementation approaches might yield different results.

To achieve this, the RFC recommends explicit reflexive mappings for all code points (even those with no non-reflexive variants), consistent assignment of types to all mappings, clear derivation rules that form a cascade (with later rules applying only to labels that did not match earlier ones), and documented explanation of any complex decisions. These practices make the LGR easier to review and its implementation easier to verify.

The formal representation of an LGR is in XML (defined in RFC 7940). The RFC shows how the examples translate: a simple character element for a code point, nested 'var' elements for each variant mapping (each with a type and optional context), and 'action' elements that form the cascade of derivation rules. The XML format directly corresponds to the abstract concepts introduced throughout the RFC.
sections.eli5: A good ruleset is clear about what it does, consistent in how it marks each rule, and easy for someone else to check and implement. The actual format is XML, but the ideas are what matter.
